working_title: Wales's Links Courses: Three Classics Worth the Drive
angle: Scotland gets all the pilgrimages, but Wales quietly delivers world-class links golf at a fraction of the cost and crowd. The post makes the practical case for a Welsh links trip built around Royal Porthcawl, Royal St David's (Harlech), and Pennard, covering what each course actually demands and why the trio work well together as a manageable self-drive itinerary.
research_notes:
- Wales has only three courses in the Top 100 GB&I rankings for 2025/26, but nine more in the Next 100 (101–200) — genuine depth at the upper end.
- Royal Porthcawl: ranked No.1 in Wales and 33rd in GB&I (Golf World, 2025); sea views from every hole; classic outer front-nine / inner back-nine routing; hosted the 2017 and 2023 Senior Open (Alex Cejka won 2023); designer credits include Ramsay Hunter (1898), H.S. Colt (1919), Martin Ebert (2011); Edward VII conferred the Royal prefix in 1909; finish hole is a 459-yard par 4 playing downhill toward the ocean; visitor tee times available with practice facilities and a traditional clubhouse; accessible off M4 junction 37. NOTE: a green fee figure (£195) appears in one 2023-flagged source — do not use as it may be outdated; describe as 'expect to pay a premium green fee' or similar.
- Royal St David's (Harlech): ranked No.2 in Wales (Golf World, 2025) and 57th in GB&I; established 1894; set beneath a UNESCO World Heritage-listed castle with Snowdonia views; course measures just over 6,600 yards from championship tees; famously demanding par (one of the toughest pars in the Top 100 UK&I); back-nine runs into the dunes from the 14th — including a long blind par-3 14th and an unusual par-3 finish at the 18th; notorious pot bunkers; rated No.1 in National Club Golfer's Top 100 Affordable Courses list (no specific fee confirmed — describe as 'relatively affordable for a Top 100 course'); dormy house available for stay-and-play packages.
- Pennard Golf Club: ranked No.3 in Wales (Golf World, 2025) and 70th in GB&I; situated on the Gower Peninsula (UK's first AONB), 8 miles west of Swansea; 200 feet above sea level, earning nickname 'the links in the sky'; founded 1896, shaped by James Braid and later C.K. Cotton; 6,225 yards, par 71; signature 7th hole (Castle) plays between the ruins of a 13th-century church and Pennard Castle; cattle occasionally graze the common land on the course; 40 well-placed bunkers; visitors welcome every day; notably wild and exposed — wind management is critical; some blind shots with limited yardage markers flagged in recent visitor reviews.
- Value angle: Wales is consistently described as significantly cheaper to play than comparable courses in Scotland or Ireland, without the same visitor volumes.
- Practical logistics: all three courses are driveable in a single trip — Porthcawl and Pennard are both in South Wales and within about an hour of each other; Royal St David's is a roughly 2.5–3 hour drive north to the Llŷn/Snowdonia coast. A logical itinerary is two nights in South Wales (Porthcawl + Pennard), then a drive north to finish at Harlech.
- No fabricated green fees, quotes, or specific yardages beyond those confirmed in research.
